title: Team Members Who Are Too Easily Intimidated
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This companion piece flips the intimidation dynamic around, focusing on team members who feel intimidated by confident or expert colleagues. It argues that intimidation, absent actual threats, is something people ultimately allow themselves to feel through comparison. The article traces how comparing one's own standing to others erodes confidence and prompts people to clam up rather than contribute. The prescribed remedy is to redirect attention toward the substance of the exchange and one's own knowledge rather than perceived rankings.
points: Even confident people can feel intimidated by colleagues who are more expert or forceful.
Unless it involves threats, intimidation is something people allow themselves to feel via comparison.
Comparing one's standing, knowledge, or success to others is the main driver of feeling intimidated.
The remedy is redirecting focus to the substance of the conversation rather than perceived rankings.
Confidence comes from contributing what one knows, not from managing how others perceive you.
quotes: For those with anxiety or lower self-esteem, intimidation can be a more frequent occurrence, resulting in a feeling of powerlessness and insecurity.
The truth is that people must give leaders or others the power to make them feel inferior. And that is actually good news.
Unless it involves threats of violence, intimidation is something that people allow themselves to feel.
Whenever a comparison pops into mind, the key is to redirect the attention to the substance of the exchange and not the people involved.
Confidence comes from the choices team members make to contribute what they can, and not from the perceptions they project onto others and themselves.
